# Module 1. What Q-CRAFT does and why it exists {#sec-m1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**In this chapter.** Run a full projection in ten minutes, before anything is explained. Then the model is built in front of you in two stages: first the base machine, a long-term fiscal projection model with no climate in it, resting on one equation and the three numbers it needs, and then the warming block, which bolts onto that finished machine at two points and makes the same equation climate-aware. The chapter closes with the parity evidence, so you can decide now whether to trust the numbers: baseline parity is exact for 147 of 147 tested countries.

Short on time: do [the ten-minute run](#sec-m1-tenminutes), [the three-number table](#sec-m1-modules) and the map at the top of [the warming block](#sec-m1-climate). Skip the rest and come back to it.
:::

## Q-CRAFT runs in a published Excel workbook, and in this Explorer

The IMF publishes Q-CRAFT as an Excel workbook, downloadable from its website. The choice was deliberate and sound: every ministry has Excel, staff know it, and a Fund tool must run in nearly two hundred countries without assuming data or infrastructure that may not be there. The workbook is well structured, clearly documented, and covers 197 economies. Three counts recur in this course, measuring different layers: the workbook's macro data covers those 197 economies, the climate dataset behind the scenarios carries 171, and the Explorer's dropdown holds the 175 present in the WEO and UN data.

**Q-CRAFT Explorer runs that same economics on the web, built so more of your hour goes on the analysis and less on carrying numbers by hand.** Four things are different:

1. Up-to-date data. A posted workbook ships with the WEO vintage it was built on, which ages between releases. The Explorer ships two data modes. Current, the default, carries the latest bundled release, WEO April 2026 as this is written. Verified carries the workbook's own WEO October 2024 vintage for checking the tool against the original. Refreshing the data is a release rather than a download and a rebuild.
2. Guidance where you need it. The help for choosing a parameter sits next to the parameter. That is the difference between reading about expenditure rigidity and choosing a value while looking at what your own country's spending has actually done, which [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) has you do.
3. Faster to the analysis. Fewer manual steps sit between the question and the chart.
4. The export packet. Your assumptions, your written remarks on them, and presentation-ready output come out together, so the record of what you decided travels with the numbers. You build one in [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd), export it in [Module 4](m4-worked-example.qmd), and hand it over in [Module 6](m6-capstone.qmd).

The Explorer runs a TypeScript port of the Python reference engine. The Python engine is verified against the workbook and the port against the Python engine ([the parity check below](#sec-m1-parity)). Both are permissively licensed open source, so anyone can examine, verify, and extend them.

::: {.callout-note}
## The workbook has its own walkthrough
The modules teach on the Explorer. The appendix [Running the official workbook](appendix-workbook.qmd) is the quick orientation to the workbook itself: the download, the Dashboard, each control mapped to the concept it sets, and where the outputs live. The IMF's User Guide remains the official manual.
:::

## Run a country in ten minutes {#sec-m1-tenminutes}

**Run the tool before you read how it works.** The explanation lands better on something you have already seen move. Six steps follow, about ten minutes in all.

The figure below is the shape of those ten minutes, one panel per stop.

{{< include figures/_m1-ten-minutes.qmd >}}

Two moves happen in the sidebar and one in each of four tabs, and the last of them produces a file you keep. Now do it.

### Zero to a projection, in six steps

[Open Q-CRAFT Explorer](https://teal-insights.github.io/QCraft-App/explorer/) and follow these steps:

1. Select a country from the sidebar dropdown. Pick the one you work on, or pick Uganda for a run checkable against a published result: it is the tool's verification country and the worked case in [Module 4](m4-worked-example.qmd). Either way, WEO macroeconomic data and UN population projections load automatically. Nothing to download, nothing to paste.
2. Leave every control at its Explorer default, and read the data banner. The sidebar footer confirms the defaults, and the banner above the tabs names what they run on: Current mode, WEO April 2026 and UN population projections 2024. That vintage is the first thing a reviewer will ask about.
3. Open the Baseline tab. This is the country's fiscal trajectory with no climate damage. The shaded band through the WEO horizon is the published record and forecast: if the latest debt-to-GDP figure there does not square with what you know about the country, work out why before going further. Then note the debt-to-GDP number at 2099.
4. Open the Climate tab. Six warming scenarios, their effect on GDP. Note where the scenarios separate, and in which year.
5. Open the Analysis tab. Baseline and all climate scenarios on one debt chart. The vertical gap between the baseline line and the Hot unadapted line is the number your fiscal risk paragraph will be about.
6. Open the Data tab and download both CSVs, the selected scenario and all scenarios together. Keep them: they are the first piece of your capstone export packet, though a run at untouched defaults is not yet a defensible one. [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) is where each of those defaults gets its line.

If you picked Uganda, you have done with five clicks the analysis ministry staff produced in a five-day workshop with a visiting IMF team in September 2023. The workshop's finding, published in the [C-PIMA](glossary.qmd#gloss-c-pima) high-level summary: GDP loss by end of century could pass 4 percentage points, with debt rising to 66 percent of GDP against 47.5 percent in the baseline [(IMF, 2024)](references.qmd#src-imf-2024-uganda).

**Your numbers will not match theirs exactly, even on the same country.** That workshop used the 2023 WEO vintage and its own parameter choices, and the Explorer's default Current mode runs WEO April 2026. Which vintage and which parameters were used is precisely what gets lost, and precisely what the export packet is for.

{{< include figures/_screenshot-m1-analysis-gap.qmd >}}

## The base machine, before any climate {#sec-m1-base}

{{< include figures/_course-map-m1.qmd >}}

The four lit nodes are the base machine, and this chapter builds it first. The warming block at the bottom of the map arrives second, and the map comes back later with only that block lit.

**Before Q-CRAFT is a climate tool it is a long-term fiscal projection model.** Give it a country and it projects the debt-to-GDP ratio to 2099 with no warming in the picture at all. It is the same machine underneath every debt sustainability analysis you have read.

Nothing below mentions climate. Warming arrives in the next section as one block that bolts on.

### One equation produces the whole debt path

Next year's debt ratio is this year's, grown by the interest rate, shrunk by economic growth, less whatever the government paid down.

That sentence is the whole model. In shorthand:

$$d_t = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + r_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $d_t$ | Debt-to-GDP ratio in year $t$ |
| $r_t$ | Effective nominal interest rate on government debt |
| $g_t$ | Nominal GDP growth rate |
| $pb_t$ | Primary balance as a share of GDP (revenue minus non-interest spending) |

Three of those four are inputs. The fourth, $d$, is the answer and also last year's input, so the tool walks the projection forward one year at a time.

**The sign of $r$ minus $g$ decides whether the ratio climbs on its own.** When interest rates exceed growth, the debt ratio rises automatically, and the government must run a primary surplus even to hold debt still. When growth exceeds interest rates, the ratio declines even with modest deficits. Step 1 of [Module 2](m2-debt-equation.qmd) works this through with numbers, and Steps 2 and 3 build the rest of the tool on top of it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## In numbers: one year of the debt dynamics equation

Start a country at a debt ratio of 60 percent of GDP, effective interest at 8 percent, nominal growth at 6 percent, and a primary deficit of 1 percent of GDP.

The amplifier goes first, meaning the factor $(1+r)/(1+g)$ that carries last year's ratio forward. 1.08 over 1.06 is 1.019, so the ratio carries forward at a little over one for one:

$$60 \times \frac{1.08}{1.06} = 61.1$$

Then the primary balance. A deficit of 1 percent of GDP is $pb = -1$, and subtracting a negative adds:

$$61.1 - (-1.0) = 62.1$$

Next year's ratio is 62.1 percent of GDP. The government borrowed one point of GDP and the ratio rose by 2.1, because the interest-growth gap supplied the other 1.1.

**Sensitivity.** Raise growth by one point, to 7 percent, and next year's ratio lands at 61.6 instead of 62.1. Half a point in one year looks like nothing. Hold the same two settings for ten years and the paths land at 83.2 and 76.3 percent of GDP. That is this course's whole climate story in advance: warming takes a fraction of a point off $g$, and the equation compounds it for seventy years.
:::

### Where the three numbers come from {#sec-m1-modules}

Growth has three suppliers, the interest rate has one rule, and the primary balance has two sides. Keep the table below beside you while you set the controls. The sections after it are for the number you happen to be arguing about.

| The number | What builds it | What you control |
|---|---|---|
| **Growth, $g$** | Working-age population, output per worker, and the price path, combined into nominal GDP growth | The UN population variant, and the productivity and inflation paths, a start and a long-run value for each |
| **Interest rate, $r$** | One of three rate rules, applied to the debt stock | The interest-rate approach: which of the three rules runs |
| **Primary balance, $pb$** | Revenue, which tracks nominal GDP, minus primary expenditure, which grows with productivity, inflation and total population, plus any fiscal rule adjustment | The debt target, and the fiscal rule on or off |

**Every one of the Explorer's ten sidebar controls, country selection included, lands on exactly one of the three numbers.** Every control starts at an Explorer default. Choosing them, and writing down why, is [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd)'s whole job.

::: {.callout-warning .authoring-note}

#### Growth, $g$, is three things multiplied together

**Growth is the number with the most suppliers, and the one your assumptions move most.**

Demography sets how fast the workforce grows.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A["UN WPP<br>variant"] --> B["Working-age<br>population"] --> C["Employment<br>growth"]
    style C fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

The workforce sets how fast the economy can grow. Q-CRAFT takes population by age group (children, working age, elderly) from UN World Population Prospects, in three variants: medium, high, and low. Growth in the working-age population, ages 15 to 64, drives employment growth after the WEO forecast horizon, and employment growth drives potential GDP. Ethiopia's working-age population is projected to keep growing for the rest of the century, pushing potential growth up and debt ratios down. Thailand's has already turned and is falling, which does the opposite before any climate damage is applied.

Productivity sets output per worker, and it moves gradually rather than in a step.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A["Start rate"] --> B["Logistic<br>convergence"] --> C["Productivity<br>growth"]
    style C fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

The measure is GDP per employed person, from World Bank data. You give the model a starting growth rate and a long-run rate, and it slides between them along an S-shaped path, which economists call a logistic curve. The curve's turning point, the year the transition is halfway, sits 15 years into the projection; the workbook lets you move it ([User Guide, p. 12, footnote 7](references.qmd#src-user-guide)) and the Explorer holds it at 15. Vietnam makes the shape concrete: a catch-up economy raising output per worker quickly now, with the rate expected to ease as the level approaches the frontier. The resulting productivity level relative to the OECD is a useful realism check, shown on the workbook's Productivity sheet and not yet in the Explorer: assumptions that imply a low-income country overtaking OECD productivity by 2099 deserve another look.

Inflation turns real growth into the nominal growth the debt ratio actually responds to.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A["WEO final<br>year rate"] --> B["Logistic<br>convergence"] --> C["Long-run<br>target"]
    style C fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

Inflation follows the same gradual S-shaped path as productivity. The starting rate should reflect the WEO projection for the final forecast year, the ending rate the long-run target: typically 2 to 3 percent for advanced economies and 3 to 6 percent for emerging and developing economies. Where the central bank publishes an explicit target, that number is the reference point.

The three combine into nominal GDP growth.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A[Employment] --> D["Nominal GDP<br>growth"]
    B[Productivity] --> D
    C[Inflation] --> D
    style D fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

The three multiply rather than add. Q-CRAFT uses the IMF's own projections through the WEO forecast period, which the tool caps at 2029. Beyond that horizon the model takes over, using the assumptions set in the dashboard. Where a country's WEO series ends earlier, the handover happens at that earlier year instead.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## In numbers: the growth decomposition

Put employment growth at 2 percent, productivity growth at 3 percent, and inflation at 5 percent.

Real growth is the first two multiplied together:

$$1.02 \times 1.03 = 1.0506$$

which is 5.06 percent. Nominal growth puts the price path on top of that:

$$1.0506 \times 1.05 = 1.1031$$

which is 10.31 percent. That is the $g$ the debt dynamics equation uses. Adding the three rates instead gives 10.00 percent. The User Guide describes nominal growth as approximately the sum of the three [(p. 25)](references.qmd#src-user-guide); the workbook computes the product, and the difference is three tenths of a point every year.

**Sensitivity.** Take one point off productivity growth, down to 2 percent, and nominal growth lands at 9.24 percent instead of 10.31. The loss is a little larger than the point you removed, because the terms multiply.
:::

#### The interest rate, $r$, is one rule applied to the debt stock

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A["Rate rule<br>(3 options)"] --> B["Effective<br>nominal rate"]
    style B fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

**This number is what carrying the debt costs.** Q-CRAFT offers three rules: a constant nominal rate, a constant gap between the interest rate and growth, or a constant real rate. Country expertise matters: the choice should reflect concessional lending terms, sovereign risk premia, and the maturity structure of domestic financial markets. For a country moving from concessional to commercial borrowing, this assumption does more work than any other. Zambia's shift into Eurobond issuance through the 2010s is the standard example, and the debt-service consequences arrived faster than any demographic or productivity trend could have.

#### The primary balance, $pb$, is revenue minus non-interest spending

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A[Revenue] --> C["Primary<br>balance"]
    B["Primary<br>expenditure"] --> C
    style C fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

**The two sides grow on different rules.** Revenue grows with nominal GDP, holding the revenue-to-GDP ratio constant. Primary expenditure, meaning spending excluding interest payments, grows multiplicatively with productivity, inflation, and total population: (1 + productivity growth) × (1 + inflation) × (1 + population growth), plus any fiscal rule adjustment. When the fiscal rule is enabled, it cuts primary expenditure by the fiscal gap when debt is above the target and rising, and loosens it when debt is below the target and falling. The target is a ceiling that debt approaches without hitting.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## In numbers: why the expenditure formula multiplies

Put productivity growth at 3 percent, inflation at 5 percent, and population growth at 2 percent. Primary expenditure of 100 units next year is

$$100 \times 1.03 \times 1.05 \times 1.02 = 110.3$$

Adding the three rates instead would give 110.0. Three tenths of a unit in the first year, which is nothing.

**Sensitivity.** The two versions keep separating, because each year's gap compounds on the last. Run both for seventy years and the multiplicative path ends about 22 percent above the additive one: a different debt projection rather than a rounding difference. The engine implements the multiplicative form.
:::

### The base machine is complete

**Two published data sources feed three manufactured numbers, and one equation turns them into the debt path.** Every sidebar control except expenditure rigidity works on this machine. Rigidity waits for the warming block. The machine works for any country in the tool, and no climate variable enters it anywhere.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: the same chain as a kitchen analogy

The pantry holds the ingredients somebody else bought: the WEO macroeconomic series and the UN population projections. In the Explorer you cannot change them, and every cook in every country works from the same shelves. The workbook lets a ministry restock the pantry with its own figures, pasted into the blue input sheets ([User Guide, pp. 9-10](references.qmd#src-user-guide)).

The seasoning is the sidebar controls, and it is yours: the demography variant, the growth assumptions, the interest-rate approach, the debt target, the fiscal rule, expenditure rigidity. They come in small quantities with large effect, and are why two cooks working from one pantry produce different dishes.

Everything the tool does before the final step is preparing growth, the interest rate and the primary balance.

The one recipe is the debt dynamics equation. The same method runs for every country, every scenario, every year.

The analogy breaks in two places: feedback and prediction. A cook tastes and adjusts. This model does not: nothing downstream feeds back into the ingredients, so cutting spending inside the model never slows growth, the partial-equilibrium limit stated below. A recipe is a claim about what comes out of the oven. A projection to 2099 is not. It is a comparison between two dishes made from deliberately different seasoning.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Two properties of the base machine worth knowing

It is partial equilibrium. The tool does not let fiscal policy feed back into GDP growth or interest rates [(User Guide, p. 5)](references.qmd#src-user-guide). That is the reason a Q-CRAFT result is a comparison rather than a forecast.

It is seven functions. Under the hood the engine composes one pure function per box in the sections above into a single call. That is a fact about the code rather than the economics. The code lives in the [repository](https://github.com/Teal-Insights/QCraft-App/tree/main/packages/qcraft-engine).
:::

## The warming block snaps on {#sec-m1-climate}

Now add one block.

{{< include figures/_course-map-m1-dock.qmd >}}

**The warming scenarios do not add a term to the equation and do not change how any of the three numbers is built.** They reach into the finished machine at two nodes. Growth falls, and where spending is rigid the primary balance weakens with it. The equation then does what it already did.

### Warming lowers growth, and weakens the primary balance when spending is rigid

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4
flowchart LR
    A["Temperature<br>path"] --> B["Productivity<br>loss"] --> C["Lower g,<br>weaker pb"]
    style C fill:#1ABC9C,stroke:#2C3E50,color:#fff
```

Lowering growth is the only way climate enters the equation. The damage estimates are empirical, drawn from the IMF Fiscal Affairs Department's FADCP Climate Dataset [(Massetti and Tagklis, 2023](references.qmd#src-massetti-2023); [Centorrino, Massetti and Tagklis, 2024)](references.qmd#src-centorrino-2024), building on the [Kahn et al. (2021)](references.qmd#src-kahn-2021) methodology for long-term macroeconomic effects of climate change. [Six scenarios](glossary.qmd#gloss-climate-scenarios) run from Paris, warming held below 2°C above pre-industrial by 2100, to Hot unadapted, high warming with very slow adaptation. Impacts begin in 2030, and before that year all scenarios match the baseline [(User Guide, p. 19)](references.qmd#src-user-guide). The channel is productivity: reduced GDP growth means lower revenue, higher expenditure-to-GDP ratios, and accelerating debt.

**The weakened primary balance is the channel people miss.** Revenue tracks nominal GDP, so a smaller economy collects less. Spending does not automatically shrink to match. The expenditure rigidity control in [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) sets how much of it does. At full rigidity the whole revenue shortfall becomes borrowing. That is why the same warming scenario produces a much wider debt fan in one country than another.

| The number | Under warming | What you control |
|---|---|---|
| **Growth, $g$** | Damage applied from 2030, rising with the temperature path | The scenario you read against baseline |
| **Primary balance, $pb$** | Revenue falls with GDP; spending falls only as far as rigidity allows | Expenditure rigidity, 0.0 to 1.0 |
| **Interest rate, $r$** | Untouched by the climate block | Nothing |

The channel is temperature, so hot low-latitude economies take the largest modelled hit. Bangladesh is exactly that kind of economy, and the one that shows what the model leaves out: sea-level rise is not in this model at all ([Module 5](m5-boundaries.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The six climate scenarios

| Scenario | Warming (wrt present, 2081-2100) | Based on | Description |
|----------|----------------------|----------|-------------|
| **Paris** | +0.7°C | SSP1-2.6 | The 2015 Paris commitments are met, with significant emission cuts; warming held below 2°C above pre-industrial at the end of the century |
| **Moderate** | +1.6°C | SSP2-4.5 | Emissions continue on present trends and stabilise at century's end; mitigation continues along the observed trend, with no more aggressive action |
| **High** | +2.5°C | SSP3-7.0 | Countries scale back their implemented policies in a fragmented world, with limited energy-efficiency gains and continued fossil fuel use |
| **Hot** | +3.5°C | SSP3-7.0, 90th percentile | Same emissions as High, using the 90th percentile of temperature increases across the climate models rather than the median |
| **Hot adapted** | +3.5°C | SSP3-7.0, 90th percentile | Same temperatures as Hot, with countries adapting more quickly (a 20-year window rather than 30) |
| **Hot unadapted** | +3.5°C | SSP3-7.0, 90th percentile | Same temperatures as Hot, with countries adapting very slowly (a 50-year window) |

The six names and the descriptions are the User Guide's [(p. 18)](references.qmd#src-user-guide). The warming column is read from the guide's Table 1, the best estimates for 2081-2100 relative to present, which the guide sources to Arias and others (2021, Cross-Section Box TS.1) [(User Guide, p. 33)](references.qmd#src-user-guide). The table's note says the figures exclude the 1.1°C of warming already reached; adding it gives the familiar above-pre-industrial framing: Paris below 2°C, Moderate about 2.7°C, High about 3.6°C, Hot about 4.6°C. Read severity from the Warming column. Hot is hotter than High, because it takes the 90th percentile of the same models whose median defines High.

Know one naming difference before a meeting. A published fiscal risk statement may report a subset of these under its own labels. The worked case in [Module 4](m4-worked-example.qmd) carries five scenarios and calls the last one "Vulnerable" rather than "Hot unadapted". Same scenario, different label, and this course uses the User Guide's names.

These scenarios are conservative in ways that matter for how you write up the results. [Module 5](m5-boundaries.qmd) sets out what they leave out.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Self-check: where does it live?

A colleague sends you five questions in one email. For each, name which of the three numbers it moves, and where the tool builds that number. Commit to your five answers before opening the panel.

1. "Our fiscal rule ceiling is 50 percent of GDP. Does the model know that?"
2. "The projection assumes we keep growing at 6 percent forever. Does it?"
3. "Why does the debt path only start diverging across scenarios in 2030?"
4. "We are shifting from IDA credits to Eurobonds. Where does that show up?"
5. "Spending per person keeps rising in the projection. Who decided that?"

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: self-check answers

Four of the five land on two of the three numbers.

1. **The primary balance.** The debt target and the fiscal rule on/off switch both sit on the spending side, and both are yours to set.
2. **Growth.** It is built from employment, productivity and inflation along a gradual path, so it does not sit at the WEO rate forever.
3. **Growth, and the primary balance behind it.** The climate scenarios move both, and impacts start in 2030 by construction, with every scenario equal to the baseline before that [(User Guide, p. 19)](references.qmd#src-user-guide).
4. **The interest rate.** The rate rule is where concessional-to-commercial transitions live. The sidebar's interest-rate approach chooses among the three rules: run all three and report the spread in your write-up.
5. **The primary balance.** Primary expenditure grows with productivity, inflation and total population, multiplicatively. Nobody decided it per person. It falls out of that formula.

If you missed 3, reread the warming section above. If you missed 5, note that the expenditure growth formula multiplies: (1 + a) × (1 + b) × (1 + c), never a + b + c.
:::
:::

## The engine is checked against the Excel workbook, and the Explorer's port against the engine {#sec-m1-parity}

A reimplementation is worth nothing if it quietly disagrees with the original. The course tells the verification story once, here, because you should decide now whether to trust the numbers.

The figure below shows the check on top and, underneath, the two claims it produces, drawn to scale against each other.

{{< include figures/_m1-parity.qmd >}}

Identical inputs go through both the original Excel workbook and the Python reference engine, and the four fiscal ratios, the interest rate, real growth and nominal GDP are compared for every projection year of the baseline. The Explorer runs a TypeScript port of that engine, and the port is checked against the Python engine on the same runs, agreeing to machine precision. The two bars differ in length because the baseline claim covers four series exactly and the climate claim stops at the ratios.

Think of the comparison as an auditor reconciling two copies of the same ledger. If a single number differs, the test fails and we investigate.

Baseline parity is exact for 147 of 147 tested countries: zero percentage-point deviation on debt-to-GDP, revenue, primary balance and primary expenditure as shares of GDP. An additional 25 parameter sensitivity combinations were tested and passed. Climate-scenario parity is confirmed for ratio metrics only, meaning debt-to-GDP, revenue and expenditure as percent of GDP, across the tested countries and scenarios.

**The climate claim covers the ratios you would quote in a Fiscal Risk Statement, not every level series in the workbook.** If your analysis turns on a climate-scenario figure in levels rather than as a share of GDP, check it against the Excel tool yourself.

The test suite is public and runs on every change, in the [engine package](https://github.com/Teal-Insights/QCraft-App/tree/main/packages/qcraft-engine) alongside the code it tests.

## What you can now do

- You have run a full projection in the Explorer for a country of your choice and exported the results. That file is capstone material.
- You can name the three numbers the equation needs and say what builds each one, and match any parameter you are asked about to the number it moves.
- You can separate the base projection model from the warming block, and name the two nodes the block attaches to.
- You can explain why a reimplementation of an Excel tool needs a parity test, say what the claim covers (baseline, 147 of 147, exact) and say what it does not (climate levels).

**The common error at this stage is treating the tool as seven things to learn.** It is one equation with three inputs, the inputs have suppliers, and warming is one block on top. If you can answer the "where does it live" self-check, you have the map.

On your desk this week: when someone hands you a fiscal projection, ask which of $r$, $g$ and $pb$ their headline number moves. The question works on projections that have nothing to do with climate.
